heading: Every member states its type
body:
Tachyon reads types to check routes, models, events and injection, and each language's checker reads them to find a mistake before a request does. A member without a type is invisible to both. So every field, method parameter and return value of a class states its type, in public and private members alike. Local variables do not need one.

Where the language's syntax has no types, a type comment carries the type. It is the one kind of comment that Tachyon keeps, because a tool reads it: it holds a type, never an explanation. Where the language has optional types, write the native types.

| Language | Parameter | Return value | Field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript | `@param {number} amount` | `@returns {Price}` | `/** @type {PriceService} */` |
| Ruby | `# @param amount [Integer]` | `# @return [Price]` | `# @return [PriceService]` above `attr_reader` |
| Lua | `---@param amount integer` | `---@return Price` | `---@type PriceService` above the field in the class table |
| Python | `amount: int` | `-> Price` | `price_service: PriceService` |
| PHP | `int $amount` | `): Price` | `private PriceService $priceService` |
| TypeScript | `amount: number` | inferred | `priceService!: PriceService` |
| Groovy | `int amount` | `Price priceFor(...)`, never `def` | `private PriceService priceService` |

JavaScript, Ruby and Lua type comments stand in the comment block right above the member; an annotation line such as `@Needs`, `#[Needs]` or `-- @Needs` may stand between them. Lua writes LuaCATS comments, which the Lua language server reads too, and a model lists its fields as `---@field amount integer` under `---@class Price`. A JavaScript method that gives back nothing needs no `@returns`; Python and PHP still write `-> None` and `: void`. A JavaScript or Python field whose starting value is one number, text or boolean, such as `static _CURRENCY = 'EUR'`, already shows its type. Groovy members need a declared type instead of `def` (`TY1334`), and the typed languages need nothing more: their tabs below use the native types. The tabs show Yon classes, but the same rule holds for Tac services when `tac.types.check` is on. Swift is a Tac service language only, so it has no tab here.

The build refuses, with `TY1356`, a member of a class in a role folder that has no type. The message names the member, and the help shows the exact comment or annotation to add. The types must also be right: `tsc` checks JavaScript types (with `checkJs` and `strict`, as in the `jsconfig.json` of `ty init`), Python and PHP check their own, and for Ruby and Lua the build checks that every name in a YARD or LuaCATS type is a Ruby class or a LuaCATS built-in type (`string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `table`), a class or model of your project, a Tachyon class, or `Boolean`, `nil` or `void`.

One `tsc` check is off for JavaScript: `strictPropertyInitialization`. TypeScript writes `priceService!: PriceService` to say that Tachyon fills the field after it makes the object. JavaScript has no `!`, so with this check `tsc` would refuse every `@Needs` field. The `jsconfig.json` that `ty init` writes for JavaScript code therefore sets `strictPropertyInitialization` to `false`, and the build checks the fields instead: in a JavaScript class, every field has a starting value, such as `labels = []`, the constructor or an `@OnStart` method sets it, or Tachyon fills it. Tachyon fills a field marked `@Needs` or `@Setting`, every field of a class marked `@NeedsAll`, the fields of an `@Entity`, and `applicationEventPublisher`. Any other field stops the build with `TY1356`, and the help shows the fixes. A side of the app that uses only TypeScript keeps the full `strict` check.

A class file may not switch the type checker off. `// @ts-nocheck`, `// @ts-ignore` and `// @ts-expect-error` in JavaScript and TypeScript, and `# type: ignore`, `# mypy: ignore-errors` and `# pyright: ignore` in Python, stop the build with `TY1356` too: remove them and fix the type errors they hid. A test file may still use `@ts-expect-error` to show that a wrong call does not compile.

`ty migrate fix --write` adds the types it can know: the type of an injected field, such as `/** @type {PriceService} */` or `# @return [PriceService]`, and `-> None` or `: void` for a method that gives back nothing. It lists every other member with the comment to add.

This check is new. It is off by default until the last examples and test projects of Tachyon pass it. Turn it on for one side of the app: for Yon code, set `types.check` to `true` in `server/application.json`, as the example below does; for Tac code, set `tac.types.check` to `true` in `client/manifest.json`. `ty migrate check` lists every place to change, even when the setting is off.

C++ has no tab here, because C++ Yon code has only route controllers so far: the build refuses `Needs` in C++ with `TY1308` (ADR 0099).
